questions.q: Galicia's vineyards are maritime on the Atlantic coast. Which climate do they turn towards as you travel inland, by the Court's Certified cell?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified climate cell reads maritime on the coast, becoming more continental moving inland. Rías Baixas takes the ocean's rain and mild temperatures; up the Sil valley in Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra the summers grow hotter and the winters colder, and Monterrei, against the Portuguese border, is the most continental of Galicia's five denominations.

questions.q: Ribeira Sacra's steep slopes are the walls of a river canyon. Which river, a tributary that joins the Miño below them, cut that canyon?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified physical feature for Galicia is the steep slopes of Ribeira Sacra. They fall to the Sil, which flows west out of Bierzo past Valdeorras and cuts a deep gorge before it meets the Miño near Ourense; the Miño itself is the Introductory river, the border with Portugal.

questions.q: What form of vineyard does the Court name for Ribeira Sacra, where the canyon walls are too steep to plant as they stand?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified grape growing cell reads terraced vineyards in Ribeira Sacra. The narrow stone-walled ledges, many first cut in Roman and monastic times, are worked by hand because no machine can reach them; the Introductory cell's high canopy trellis belongs to rainy Rías Baixas on the coast.

questions.q: Which soil type does the Court's Certified cell give for Galicia, the rock that underlies Rías Baixas?
questions.exp: The Court gives one soil for Galicia at the Certified level: granite. In Rías Baixas it weathers into a coarse, sandy, acidic topsoil that drains quickly, the counterweight to more than 1,600 millimetres of rain a year; chalk and limestone belong to Champagne and Rioja Alavesa, basalt to volcanic islands.

questions.q: Galician whites are made with modern technology in stainless steel. What does the Court's Certified winemaking cell add to that picture?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified cell reads occasional barrique (barrica) use. Most Albariño stays in steel on its fine lees, but a Rías Baixas Barrica label marks a wine with at least three months in oak, and inland Godello repays a little wood; carbonic maceration, fortification and the solera belong to other wines.

questions.q: Besides Albariño, which white grape does the Court add for Galicia at the Certified level?
questions.exp: Godello is the Court's Certified white grape for Galicia and the white of Valdeorras, where it was almost lost by the 1970s before growers replanted it. It is broader, stonier and less aromatic than Albariño, and the same vine is Gouveio in Portugal's Douro.

questions.q: How does the Court describe the Godello of Valdeorras in its Certified style cell?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified style cell reads fresh and neutral Godello in Valdeorras, within dry, crisp white wines and light red wines for inland Galicia. Godello is palate driven rather than perfumed, so its interest is texture and stony weight, which lees ageing and a little oak build on.

questions.q: Ribeira Sacra DO is best known for red wine. Which two white grapes does the Court list for it?
questions.exp: The Court lists Ribeira Sacra's whites as Albariño and Godello and its red as Mencía. Verdejo and Viura are Rueda and Rioja grapes, Xarel-lo and Parellada belong to Cava, and Hondarrabi Zuri is the Basque Txakoli grape.

questions.q: Valdeorras DO is famous for its white wine, yet the Court also lists it for red. Which grape makes that red?
questions.exp: The Court lists Valdeorras for white Godello and red Mencía, and Ribeira Sacra for red Mencía with white Albariño and Godello. Mencía, the same vine as Portugal's Jaen, gives fragrant, light, red-fruited wines on the slate and granite of the Sil valley.

questions.q: Pazo Señorans, Granbazán and Lagar de Cervera are the Court's named producers of which Galician wine?
questions.exp: All three are Rías Baixas Albariño houses: Pazo Señorans at Meis and Granbazán in Val do Salnés, and Lagar de Cervera in O Rosal at the mouth of the Miño. The Court asks a Certified candidate to recognise them and to sell their wine with food.

questions.q: Which dish best meets the classic pairing the Court gives for Rías Baixas Albariño?
questions.exp: The Court calls Albariño a classic match for simply prepared shellfish and bivalves because of its coastal origin, crisp acidity and delicate flavour. Steamed mussels, oysters or grilled octopus meet its salt and citrus; oxtail and venison need tannin, and chocolate needs sweetness.
